Reduce the network to one capacitance, then use **U = ½CV²**.
**Step 1 — read the circuit.** The 6 µF and 3 µF are in **series** with each other, and
that combination is in **parallel** with the 2 µF across the 2 V supply ✓
**Step 2 — combine the series pair.**
1/C_s = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = **3/6**
C_s = **2 µF** ✓
**Step 3 — add the parallel branch.**
C = 2 + 2 = **4 µF** ✓
**Step 4 — find the energy.**
U = ½CV² = ½(4 x 10⁻⁶)(2)² ✓
= ½(4 x 10⁻⁶)(4)
= **8 x 10⁻⁶ J = 8 µJ** ✓
**Why series capacitors combine reciprocally.** They carry the **same charge**, and the
voltages add ✓ so V = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂ and 1/C_s = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. The combination is always
**smaller** than either - here 2 µF, less than both 6 and 3.
**Why parallel capacitors simply add.** They share the **same voltage**, and the charges
add ✓ C_p = C₁ + C₂. The opposite of resistors, which is worth fixing firmly in mind.
**The branch-by-branch check.**
**2 µF branch**: Q = CV = 4 µC, U = ½(2)(4) = **4 µJ** ✓
**series branch**: C_s = 2 µF, Q = 4 µC, U = ½(2)(4) = **4 µJ** ✓
total = **8 µJ** ✓ confirming the answer.
**How the series branch divides its voltage.** With Q = 4 µC common to both:
across 6 µF: V = 4/6 = **0·67 V** ✓
across 3 µF: V = 4/3 = **1·33 V** ✓
sum **2 V** ✓ The **smaller** capacitor takes the **larger** share - which is why it is
the one at risk of breakdown.
**The three forms of the energy formula.**
U = ½CV² = **½QV** = **Q²/2C** ✓ all equivalent through Q = CV; choose whichever
variables are given.
**Where the energy is stored.** In the **electric field** between the plates ✓ with
energy density u = ½ε₀E². The capacitor is a field-energy reservoir, not a charge
reservoir - it holds zero **net** charge at all times.
**Why the factor of a half.** The capacitor charges **gradually**: the first charge
crosses at zero voltage, the last at V ✓ Integrating ∫V dq = ∫(q/C)dq gives Q²/2C.
Half the energy drawn from the battery is dissipated in the resistance of the circuit,
whatever its value.
**Reading the distractors.** **16 µJ** ✗ uses C = 8 µF - adding all three in parallel
would give 11 µF, and 8 comes from some other slip. **4 µJ** ✗ is one branch alone, and
**2 µJ** ✗ uses C = 1 µF ✓
∴ 8 μJ.

Find the input power, take the half that survives, and divide by the secondary
voltage.
**Step 1 — find the input power.**
P_p = V_pI_p = 220 x 5 ✓
= **1100 W** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the 50% loss.**
P_s = 0·5 x 1100
= **550 W** ✓
**Step 3 — find the secondary current.**
I_s = P_s/V_s = 550/2200 ✓
= **0·25 A** ✓
**Why the simple relation V_pI_p = V_sI_s fails here.** That holds only for an **ideal**
transformer, 100% efficient ✓ It would give I_s = 1100/2200 = 0·5 A - which is the
fourth option, and the trap. With half the power lost, the real current is half that
again.
**The turns ratio.**
N_s/N_p = V_s/V_p = 2200/220 = **10** ✓ a **step-up** transformer, ten times as many
turns on the secondary.
**Why the voltage ratio is unaffected by the losses.** The voltages are set by the
**turns ratio** through Faraday's law, V ∝ N ✓ Losses reduce the **current** that can be
delivered, not the open-circuit voltage.
**Where the 550 W goes.** Four mechanisms ✓
**copper losses**: I²R heating in the windings
**iron losses**: hysteresis in the core, reduced by using soft iron
**eddy currents**: minimised by **laminating** the core
**flux leakage**: field lines that miss the secondary, reduced by winding one coil over
the other
**Why 50% is unrealistically bad.** Real power transformers reach **98-99%** ✓ The
figure is chosen here to make the arithmetic clear, not to describe a real machine.
**Why transformers matter.** Power is transmitted at **high voltage** to keep I small,
since the line loss is **I²R** ✓ Raising the voltage tenfold cuts the transmission loss
a hundredfold - the entire reason for the a.c. grid.
**Why they work only on a.c.** Induction requires a **changing** flux ✓ A steady direct
current produces a constant flux and no secondary e.m.f. at all - the practical argument
that settled the "war of the currents" in a.c.'s favour.
**A check on the direction of the trade.** Voltage up by 10, so current down by **at
least** 10 ✓ 5 A becomes at most 0·5 A, and with losses 0·25 A. Energy can never be
gained.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·5 A** ✗ is the ideal-transformer answer, ignoring the
loss. **5 A** ✗ supposes the current unchanged, and **2·5 A** ✗ is ten times too
large ✓
∴ 0.25 A.

Equal wavelength means equal **momentum**, and with K = p²/2m the **lighter** particle
has the greater energy.
**Step 1 — use the de Broglie relation.**
λ = h/p, so equal λ means **equal p** ✓
**Step 2 — write the kinetic energy in terms of momentum.**
K = ½mv² = **p²/2m** ✓
**Step 3 — compare.** With p the same,
K ∝ **1/m** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** The electron is about **1836** times lighter, so its kinetic
energy is **1836 times greater** - **more than that of a proton** ✓
**The ratio.**
K_e/K_p = m_p/m_e = **1836** ✓
**A worked instance.** Take λ = 1 Å, so p = h/λ = **6·63 x 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹**:
electron: K = p²/2m_e = **2·4 x 10⁻¹⁷ J = 150 eV** ✓
proton: K = **1·3 x 10⁻²⁰ J = 0·082 eV** ✓
ratio **1830** ✓ as expected.
**Why the speeds differ so much too.** v = p/m ✓ so the electron moves 1836 times
faster: 7·3 x 10⁶ m s⁻¹ against 4·0 x 10³ m s⁻¹ for the proton.
**Why this matters in practice.** To reach the 1 Å wavelengths needed for diffraction,
electrons need only **tens of volts** while protons need a far smaller energy but are
much harder to handle ✓ This is why **electron** diffraction and electron microscopy
became the standard tools.
**The contrast with equal kinetic energy.** Then
λ = h/√(2mK) ✓ and the **heavier** particle has the **shorter** wavelength. The electron
would then have the longer λ, by a factor √1836 = **43** - the reverse comparison, and a
common source of confusion.
**The thermal-neutron comparison.** A neutron at room temperature has K ≈ 0·025 eV and
λ ≈ **1·8 Å** ✓ conveniently matching atomic spacings, which is why neutron diffraction
is used for crystallography without any acceleration at all.
**Why zero is impossible.** A finite wavelength means a finite momentum, hence a finite
energy ✓ Only a particle with λ → ∞ could have zero kinetic energy.
**The relativistic caveat.** At 150 eV the electron's speed is 2·4% of c ✓ so the
non-relativistic formula is fine here. Above a few keV the full expression
E² = p²c² + m²c⁴ is needed.
**Reading the distractors.** **Less than** ✗ inverts the 1/m dependence. **Equal to** ✗
would require equal masses, and **zero** ✗ contradicts the finite wavelength ✓
∴ more than that of a proton.

In a series RC circuit the voltages are **90° out of phase**, so they add in
**quadrature**.
**Step 1 — recall the phase relation.** The voltage across the **resistor** is in phase
with the current; the voltage across the **capacitor** lags it by **90°** ✓
**Step 2 — add as perpendicular vectors.**
V = **√(V_R² + V_C²)** ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.**
V = √(12² + 5²)
= √(144 + 25)
= **√169** ✓
**Step 4 — evaluate.**
V = **13 V** ✓
**Why they do not simply add to 17 V.** The two voltages reach their peaks at
**different instants** ✓ V_R peaks when the current peaks; V_C peaks a quarter-cycle
later, when the charge is greatest. A voltmeter across the whole circuit therefore reads
less than the arithmetic sum - 13 V, not 17 V.
**Why the capacitor voltage lags.** The charge is the **integral** of the current ✓ and
integrating a sine gives a negative cosine - a quarter-cycle behind. Physically, the
capacitor must be **charged** before a voltage appears across it.
**The phase angle of the circuit.**
tan φ = V_C/V_R = 5/12 ✓
φ = **22·6°**, with the current **leading** the applied voltage ✓ - the signature of a
capacitive circuit.
**The 5-12-13 triangle.** A Pythagorean triple ✓ chosen deliberately so the answer is
exact. Spotting it saves the arithmetic.
**The impedance.** If the current is I,
Z = V/I, R = 12/I, X_C = 5/I ✓
so Z = **√(R² + X_C²)** - the same triangle, drawn in ohms rather than volts.
**The power factor.**
cos φ = R/Z = **12/13 = 0·923** ✓ and the power dissipated is VI cos φ, all of it in the
resistor. The **capacitor dissipates none** - it stores energy for a quarter cycle and
returns it.
**The companion case, RL.** The inductor voltage **leads** by 90°, and the same
quadrature addition applies ✓ In a full RLC circuit, V_L and V_C are **antiphase** and
partly cancel: V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²).
**Why the voltages can exceed the supply in RLC.** At resonance V_L and V_C can each be
many times V while cancelling each other ✓ an alarming but real effect, and the basis of
tuned circuits.
**Reading the distractors.** **17 V** ✗ adds them arithmetically, ignoring the phase -
the classic error. **12 V** ✗ and **5 V** ✗ take one component alone ✓
∴ 13 V.

Since λ = h/√(2mK), tripling K multiplies λ by **1/√3**.
**Step 1 — write the wavelength in terms of energy.**
p = √(2mK), so
λ = h/p = **h/√(2mK)** ✓
**Step 2 — see the dependence.**
λ ∝ **1/√K** ✓
**Step 3 — triple the energy.**
λ′/λ = √(K/3K) = **1/√3** ✓
**Why the square root.** Energy depends on the **square** of the momentum ✓ so a given
factor in K produces only its square root in p, and hence in 1/λ. Tripling the energy
raises the momentum by just **73%**.
**A worked instance.** An electron at 100 eV:
λ = 12·27/√100 = **1·227 Å** ✓
at 300 eV: λ = 12·27/√300 = **0·708 Å** ✓
ratio 0·708/1·227 = **0·577 = 1/√3** ✓
**The convenient formula.** For an electron accelerated through V volts,
λ = **12·27/√V Å** ✓ which turns most such questions into one division, and is the
formula behind the Davisson-Germer analysis.
**Why the wavelength shortens as the energy rises.** Faster means more momentum, and
λ = h/p ✓ This is exactly why **electron microscopes** use high accelerating voltages:
at 100 kV, λ = 0·037 Å, giving resolution thousands of times better than visible light.
**The three proportionalities worth keeping straight.**
λ ∝ **1/v** at fixed mass ✓
λ ∝ **1/p** always ✓
λ ∝ **1/√K** for a given particle ✓
**For particles of different mass at the same energy.** λ ∝ 1/√m ✓ so a proton at a given
energy has a wavelength 43 times shorter than an electron's - which is why proton
microscopy, were it practical, would resolve even finer detail.
**The relativistic correction.** Above about **50 keV** for an electron the simple
formula errs by more than a per cent ✓ and λ = hc/√(K² + 2Kmc²) must be used. At 100 kV
the correction is about 5%.
**Why this matters for the uncertainty principle.** Δx Δp ≳ ℏ ✓ A shorter wavelength
means a larger momentum and so a finer position resolution - the same statement in two
languages.
**Reading the distractors.** **√3** ✗ and **3** ✗ make the wavelength **grow** with
energy, inverting λ = h/p. **1/3** ✗ forgets the square root ✓
∴ 1/√3.

Einstein's equation, written in wavelengths: **K = hc(1/λ − 1/λ₀)**.
**Step 1 — write the photoelectric equation.**
K_max = **hν − φ** ✓
**Step 2 — express both terms in wavelengths.**
hν = **hc/λ** ✓
φ = **hc/λ₀** ✓ since λ₀ is the threshold - the longest wavelength that just liberates an
electron with no energy to spare.
**Step 3 — subtract.**
K = hc/λ − hc/λ₀
= **hc(1/λ − 1/λ₀)** ✓
**Step 4 — put over a common denominator.**
= hc(λ₀ − λ)/(λλ₀)
= **hc[(λ₀ − λ)/(λλ₀)]** ✓
**Why λ < λ₀ is stipulated.** Only then is the photon energy **above** the work
function ✓ For λ > λ₀ the bracket turns negative, which simply means **no emission**:
there is no such thing as negative kinetic energy.
**A dimensional check.** hc has units **J m** ✓ and (λ₀ − λ)/(λλ₀) has units **1/m** ✓
so the product is an energy. The first option, hc(λ₀ − λ), would be J m² - plainly
wrong, and the fastest way to eliminate it.
**A worked instance.** Silver, λ₀ = **262 nm** (φ = 4·73 eV), illuminated at 200 nm:
K = 1240/200 − 1240/262 = 6·20 − 4·73 = **1·47 eV** ✓
by the bracketed form: 1240(62)/(200 x 262) = **1·47 eV** ✓ the same.
**The useful constant.** hc = **1240 eV nm** ✓ so energies in eV follow directly from
wavelengths in nanometres.
**Why silver needs ultraviolet.** Its work function of 4·73 eV corresponds to 262 nm ✓
well short of the visible range, so no visible light whatever will eject electrons from
silver - however intense.
**What the three key observations are.**
**threshold**: no emission below ν₀, whatever the intensity ✓
**instantaneous**: emission within 10⁻⁹ s ✓
**energy from frequency**: intensity governs the **number** of electrons, not their
speed ✓
All three defeat the wave theory and all three follow from this one equation.
**The stopping potential.**
eV₀ = K_max ✓ so V₀ = (hc/e)(1/λ − 1/λ₀), and plotting V₀ against 1/λ gives a straight
line of slope **hc/e** - Millikan's method of measuring **h**, which earned him the
1923 Nobel Prize.
**Reading the distractors.** **hc(λ₀ − λ)** ✗ fails dimensionally. **hc/(λ₀ − λ)** ✗ is
not a difference of two energies at all, and **(h/c)[(λ₀ − λ)/λλ₀]** ✗ divides by c
where it should multiply ✓
∴ hc[(λ₀ − λ)/(λλ₀)].

All the kinetic energy is spent climbing the potential hill; set up the energy balance
and solve for the distance.
**Step 1 — find the potential at C, the midpoint.** Each charge is **3 m** away:
V_C = 2 x (9 x 10⁹)(5 x 10⁻⁶)/3 ✓
= 2 x 1·5 x 10⁴ = **3 x 10⁴ V** ✓
**Step 2 — write the potential at D, a distance x from C.** By Pythagoras each charge is
√(9 + x²) away:
V_D = 2 x (9 x 10⁹)(5 x 10⁻⁶)/√(9 + x²)
= **9 x 10⁴/√(9 + x²)** ✓
**Step 3 — apply conservation of energy.** The charge starts with K = 0·06 J at C and
stops at D:
K + qV_C = **qV_D** ✓ with q = **−5 x 10⁻⁶ C**
**Step 4 — substitute.**
0·06 + (−5 x 10⁻⁶)(3 x 10⁴) = (−5 x 10⁻⁶)(9 x 10⁴/√(9 + x²))
0·06 − 0·15 = −0·45/√(9 + x²) ✓
**Step 5 — simplify.**
−0·09 = −0·45/√(9 + x²)
√(9 + x²) = 0·45/0·09 = **5** ✓
**Step 6 — solve.**
9 + x² = 25
x² = 16
**x = 4 m** ✓
**Why the negative charge slows down as it moves away.** It is **attracted** by both
positive charges ✓ Moving off the line, it climbs a potential-energy hill, and its
kinetic energy is converted into potential energy until it halts.
**The energy bookkeeping.**
U_C = qV_C = **−0·15 J** ✓
U_D = qV_D = (−5 x 10⁻⁶)(9 x 10⁴/5) = **−0·09 J** ✓
ΔU = **+0·06 J** ✓ exactly the kinetic energy surrendered.
**The 3-4-5 triangle.** With CD = 4 m and half the separation 3 m, each charge is **5 m**
from D ✓ The numbers are chosen so that the arithmetic closes neatly.
**What happens next.** It does not stay at D ✓ The attraction pulls it back, and it
oscillates through C to a symmetric point 4 m on the other side - simple harmonic only
for small displacements, anharmonic here.
**Why potentials are easier than forces.** Potential is a **scalar** ✓ The two
contributions simply add, with no components to resolve. Working this problem with
Coulomb forces would require integrating a varying force along the path.
**Why the perpendicular direction matters.** By symmetry the two forces' components
along AB **cancel** ✓ leaving a net force along DC - directed back towards C, as the
oscillation requires.
**Reading the distractors.** **3 m** ✗ would give √(9+9) = 4·24, not 5. **√3** ✗ and
**3√3 m** ✗ match no step of the energy balance ✓
∴ 4 m.

With r = √(2mK)/(qB), the alpha particle's extra mass and extra charge **cancel
exactly**.
**Step 1 — write the radius in a magnetic field.**
r = **mv/(qB)** = **p/(qB)** ✓
**Step 2 — express p through the kinetic energy.**
p = **√(2mK)** ✓
so r = **√(2mK)/(qB)** ✓
**Step 3 — form the ratio at equal K and B.**
r_α/r_p = (√m_α/q_α) ÷ (√m_p/q_p)
= **(√(m_α/m_p)) x (q_p/q_α)** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute the numbers.** The alpha particle has m = **4m_p** and q = **2e** ✓
= √4 x (1/2)
= 2 x 0·5
= **1** ✓
**Step 5 — conclude.** The ratio is **1 : 1** ✓ - the two paths have the same radius.
**Why the cancellation is exact.** The mass enters as **√m** and the charge as **1/q** ✓
Four times the mass gives a factor 2; twice the charge gives a factor ½. The alpha
particle is a helium nucleus - 4 nucleons, 2 protons - and those are precisely the
numbers that make the product unity.
**A worked instance.** At K = 1 MeV in B = 1 T:
proton: p = √(2 x 1·67 x 10⁻²⁷ x 1·6 x 10⁻¹³) = 2·31 x 10⁻²⁰, r = **0·144 m** ✓
alpha: p = √(2 x 6·68 x 10⁻²⁷ x 1·6 x 10⁻¹³) = 4·62 x 10⁻²⁰, q = 3·2 x 10⁻¹⁹,
r = **0·144 m** ✓ identical.
**Why the path is a circle.** The magnetic force **qv x B** is always perpendicular to
the velocity ✓ so it changes the direction but never the speed, providing exactly the
centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r.
**The period, which is different.**
T = **2πm/(qB)** ✓ independent of speed - the cyclotron principle. For the alpha,
T = 2π(4m)/(2eB) = **twice** the proton's, so although the circles coincide, the alpha
takes twice as long to go round.
**Why no work is done.** F ⊥ v, so F·v = 0 ✓ The kinetic energy is unchanged, which is
why a magnetic field alone can never accelerate a particle in the sense of speeding it
up - the cyclotron's **electric** gaps do that.
**The deuteron, for comparison.** m = 2m_p, q = e:
r_d/r_p = √2/1 = **1·41** ✓ a wider circle, since its charge did not keep pace with its
mass.
**Where this is used.** **Mass spectrometry** ✓ r = √(2mK)/(qB) separates ions by m/q²
at fixed energy, which is how isotopes are identified and how the first measurements of
atomic masses were made.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 2** ✗ uses the charge ratio alone; **1 : 4** ✗ the
mass ratio; **1 : 8** ✗ the product of both ✓ Only the full expression, with its square
root, gives unity.
∴ 1 : 1.
